solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Create bad upset having released tension

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so these letters are tipped into a new order

parts.note: the nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone throws a tantrum and causes a scene once the pressure inside them finally gives way.
explanation.walkthrough: To abreact is a psychoanalytic term: to discharge repressed emotion by reliving the experience that caused it.
explanation.definitionFit: Abreacting means letting out pent-up emotion, so having abreacted is having discharged built-up psychological strain.

clue.text: Addiction recovery group quiet after turning over new leaf

indicators.note: turning something over puts its end first, so the group and the quiet sign are read backwards

parts.note: Alcoholics Anonymous
p, piano, is the musical mark for quiet
standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A recovering addict joins a support group and quietly resolves to turn over a new leaf.
explanation.walkthrough: AA with P placed after it is turned round, and N then follows. 'Turning over a new leaf' is the idiom the surface rests on; only 'leaf' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Paan is the betel leaf, chewed in South Asia wrapped around areca nut and spices.

clue.text: Boy had a good time out of bounds

indicators.note: the bounds of a word are its two ends, and being out of them means both outer letters are dropped

parts.note: partied: celebrated, had fun

explanation.surface: A lad enjoyed himself somewhere he was forbidden to go.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the first and last letters of PARTIED leaves ARTIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Artie is a boy's name, a pet form of Arthur, and crosswords freely define male names as boy.

clue.text: One into cold Fosters for refreshment? He's plastered!

indicators.note: a refreshment here is a re-freshening, a making over anew, so the letters are given a fresh arrangement

parts.note: Roman numeral one
C for cold, as on a tap
the lager brand taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinker who enjoys a cold Fosters for refreshment ends up drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastered' looks like drunkenness to match the lager, but a frescoist paints on wet plaster, so the plaster is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A frescoist paints frescoes on fresh lime plaster, so his work leaves walls covered in painted plaster.

clue.text: Must find a recipe for an epicure

indicators.note: must is a variant of musth, the frenzied state of a bull elephant, so the letters are in a wild state

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for recipe, as on prescriptions

explanation.surface: A cook is told to dig out a recipe for a guest who is a gourmet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Must' reads as an obligation, but here it is the elephant's frenzy (musth). Friand is also a small French cake, but here it is the older noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Friand, from French, is an old word for a dainty person who relishes good food, a gourmet.

clue.text: Form into sphere given by lecturer sharing English award

parts.note: standard abbreviation
L for lecturer
Order of the British Empire, an honour

explanation.surface: A lecturer splits a prize with a colleague from the English department.
explanation.walkthrough: The lecturer sits between English and the award, sharing the space with both.
explanation.definitionFit: To englobe is to enclose in or shape into a globe, that is a round ball.

clue.text: Glasses very good during Ascot jumping

indicators.note: during means within a span, so one piece sits inside the other
jumping letters leap out of their places and land in a new order

parts.note: the racecourse taken as written
pi is slang for pious, very good

explanation.surface: Drinks are excellent at Royal Ascot while the horses are over the fences.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a flat-racing course, so 'jumping' is a surface trap as well as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A copita is a tulip-shaped sherry glass, so copitas are drinking vessels.

clue.text: Middle-Easterner briefly laid up

indicators.note: in a down clue, something laid up is set upward, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: in a mo, short for in a moment

explanation.surface: A man from the Middle East was briefly ill in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' looks like a time adverb in the surface, but it is the phrase 'in a mo' as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: An Omani is a native of Oman, a country of the Arabian peninsula in the Middle East.

clue.text: Was a dictator and charged by the sound of it

indicators.note: judging by the sound of a word means going on how it is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: charged with a crime; the C is silent

explanation.surface: A tyrant ruled and was then prosecuted for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' suggests a tyrant, but it means one who dictates words for writing, which is what indite once meant.
explanation.definitionFit: To indite is to compose or dictate a text, so a person who indited was one dictating words.

clue.text: Like this present? Me too

parts.note: same: identical to this
here: present, in attendance

explanation.surface: Someone admires a gift and says they would like one just like it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift, but it is the adjective meaning in attendance.
explanation.definitionFit: Same here is an informal reply agreeing that the speaker feels or does likewise.

clue.text: Rod hurried through Colombia for a deep gorge

parts.note: a bar is a rod
ran through, went quickly through
CO is Colombia's international code

explanation.surface: A man named Rod rushes across Colombia to reach a ravine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rod' sits capitalised at the start, looking like a name.
explanation.definitionFit: A barranco is a steep-sided ravine, a Spanish word used for gullies in Spanish-speaking lands.

clue.text: Greek currency regularly used on first day of the week

definitions.note: currency as a mass noun covers the plural coins

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.words: on first day of the week
parts.note: on the first day of the week is Mondays, as in 'Mondays, the shop shuts'

explanation.surface: Ancient Greek money was spent at the start of each week.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking letters one, three, five and seven of MONDAYS gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The mna, or mina, was an ancient Greek unit of weight and money worth a hundred drachmas.

clue.text: Appraisals of brass in Joplin pieces

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: Scott Joplin composed ragtime pieces, rags
both brass and tin are slang for money

explanation.surface: A critic reviews the horn section in Scott Joplin's compositions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' looks like the instruments, but it is the slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratings are assessments placing something on a scale, so they are evaluations of worth.

clue.text: Two parents shopping months for a sacred flower

indicators.note: shopping is taking goods in, so the second parent takes the other piece inside

parts.note: pa and da, two words for a father
m is the abbreviation for months

explanation.surface: A couple spend months buying a holy bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: The two parents are both fathers, PA and DA, and M goes inside the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Padma is Sanskrit for the lotus, the flower sacred in Hindu and Buddhist tradition.

clue.text: British actor returned for old computer

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Michael Caine, the British film star

explanation.surface: A British actor came back to play an outdated computer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a casting story; the actor's surname simply runs backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: ENIAC, built in 1945, was one of the first general-purpose electronic digital computers.

clue.text: Old Turkish minister with change of direction: more knitting together!

indicators.note: a change of direction swaps one compass point for its opposite

parts.note: visier is a variant spelling of vizier, an Ottoman minister

explanation.surface: An Ottoman minister changes course and sits down to more knitting.
explanation.walkthrough: The S (south) in VISIER becomes N (north). 'Knitting' suggests needles, but it is the twining of climbing vines.
explanation.definitionFit: Viny means full of or like vines, plants whose tendrils twine and interlace; vinier is more so.

clue.text: Novice put down 50 per cent? Wrong stake for this horse!

indicators.note: putting down half of something cuts it by fifty per cent, so half its letters go

parts.note: a tyro is a beginner
a sin is a wrong
an ante is a stake in poker

explanation.surface: A beginner bets on the wrong horse and loses half the stake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put down' suggests an animal destroyed, but it halves TYRO to RO.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosinante is Don Quixote's bony old nag, and the name is used for any worn-out horse.

clue.text: Clean up one side of field in French town

indicators.note: cleaning up a room shifts things about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
in cricket the field has an on side and an off side

explanation.surface: A farmer tidies one edge of a field in France.
explanation.walkthrough: The on side is the leg side of a cricket field, the half the batsman's legs face.
explanation.definitionFit: Alençon is a town in Normandy, famous for its needle lace.

clue.text: Class learns a term for Greek coffins? Could be these

indicators.note: to class is to sort, so the letters are sorted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a term is an end point, so only the final letter of the following word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A class of pupils learns the word for Greek burial chests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek' does double duty: it gives its last letter and also tells you the coffins are Greek, which 'Could be these' points at.
explanation.definitionFit: A larnax is an ancient Greek chest or box used as a burial casket; larnakes is its Greek plural.

clue.text: Worker on demand is a Scottish fellow

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits below it, so the worker is placed second

parts.note: a call is a demand, as in no call for it
the worker ant

explanation.surface: An employee who is always on call is a Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, the worker 'on' the demand sits below it, so CALL comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Callant is a Scots word for a lad or young fellow.

clue.text: Wrinkled retainer close to a corporation?

definitions.text: Wrinkled retainer close to a corporation?

parts.words: Wrinkled retainer close to a corporation?
parts.note: surface reading: an aged servant working near a company or a town council; setter's reading: a creased pouch that holds something, sited near a pot belly, corporation being old slang for a paunch

explanation.surface: An old servant of long standing works near a big company.
explanation.walkthrough: Corporation is old slang for a large belly, and retainer means something that holds, not a servant.
explanation.definitionFit: The scrotum is the wrinkled skin pouch that holds the testes, located just below the abdomen.

clue.text: Indian brother mostly scoffs no end of rather mild curries

indicators.note: mostly means all but a little, so the word loses its final letter
no end of means without the last letter of the following word, so that letter is struck out

parts.note: bhai is Hindi for brother
jeers: mocks, scoffs
the final letter of rather, which is removed

explanation.surface: A man's brother greedily eats most of the gentler curries on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffs' looks like greedy eating, but it means mocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Bhajees are spiced vegetable dishes or fritters in Indian cooking, often milder than many curries.

clue.text: Heavy particle one's not seen on satellite

indicators.note: not seen on a thing means absent from it, so that letter is missing

parts.note: Hyperion is a moon of Saturn
Roman numeral one, which is taken away

explanation.surface: A dense particle cannot be detected on a moon.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the I from HYPERION to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A hyperon is a baryon heavier than the proton and neutron, containing at least one strange quark.

clue.text: Afternoon out dancing, Ena and Tracy like electroclash?

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and settle in a new arrangement
out means gone away, so the afternoon's letter is taken away

parts.note: A for afternoon, as in p.m. timetables; removed
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two women, Ena and Tracy, spend an afternoon out dancing to electronic music.
explanation.walkthrough: The A of ENA goes, then EN and TRACY are shuffled. The question mark flags electroclash as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Electroclash is an electronic dance genre that borrows from trance music's hypnotic synth style, so it can be called trancey.

clue.text: Composer tense for jury decision

parts.note: Giuseppe Verdi, the Italian opera composer
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A musician is anxious as he awaits the court's verdict.
explanation.walkthrough: Verdit is an old spelling of verdict.
explanation.definitionFit: A verdict is the finding a jury delivers at the end of a trial; verdit is an obsolete form.

clue.text: Scottish quarter's put up a fine line

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting a word up stacks it from bottom to top, so it reads backwards

parts.note: airt is Scots for a direction or quarter of the compass; quarter's stands for quarter is, giving the plural form

explanation.surface: A Scottish district has drawn a thin boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: An airt is one of the four points of the compass in Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: A stria is a narrow streak or groove, one of a series of parallel lines on a surface.

clue.text: Forecasters of spring correct mostly

indicators.note: mostly means all but a little, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: a spa is a mineral spring
to emend is to correct a text

explanation.surface: Weather forecasters for the spring season are largely right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season but it is a water source.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaeman is Scots for a soothsayer, one who spaes, or foretells the future.

clue.text: Old Glaswegian poet with little money for day in the capital

indicators.note: one letter for another means it stands in its place

parts.note: Dakar is the capital of Senegal
m, short for a monetary unit such as the mark
D for day, which is replaced

explanation.surface: A poet from Glasgow spent a day in the capital with hardly any cash.
explanation.walkthrough: The D of DAKAR gives way to M. Makar is the Scots word for a poet; Scotland now appoints a national Makar.
explanation.definitionFit: Makar is Scots for a maker, used especially of a poet or bard.

clue.text: Fellow adopting high tone for English chemist

indicators.note: adopting means taking in, so the fellow holds the other piece inside

parts.note: a don is a university fellow
alt is a high tone in music, as in in alt

explanation.surface: A colleague puts on a lofty manner to impersonate a scientist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' suggests just a man, but it is a college fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: John Dalton was the English chemist who developed modern atomic theory.

clue.text: A mouth organ with backing in capital

indicators.note: backing means moving back, so the words are read from the end

parts.note: taken as written
harp is slang for a harmonica

explanation.surface: A harmonica player has musical accompaniment in a big city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like musical accompaniment, but it turns the letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: Praha is the Czech name for Prague, capital of the Czech Republic.

clue.text: It can be confused with "sh"

indicators.note: confused letters are mixed up and can come out in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning that two easily muddled words might be mistaken for a request to hush.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the answer is an interjection easily mistaken for the hushing sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Hist is an old exclamation demanding silence or attention, much like shush.

clue.text: Take cracking game bird from the Highlands

indicators.note: cracking something open lets a piece in, so one sits inside the other

parts.note: skat is a three-handed card game
R, recipe, Latin for take

explanation.surface: Shoot a game bird in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game bird' seems to run together, but game is the card game and bird starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Skart, or scart, is a Scots word for a cormorant or shag.

clue.text: Brother catty about daughter gets the boot

parts.note: short for brother
D for daughter
the catty is an Asian unit of weight, also called a kin

explanation.surface: A spiteful sibling is dismissive about his niece and gets sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catty' looks like spite but is a weight, and 'gets the boot' suggests dismissal.
explanation.definitionFit: A brodkin, or brodekin, is an old word for a buskin or half-boot.

clue.text: Return of swine flu revealing the spirit of Goans

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the run is read backwards
revealing means showing what was tucked inside, so the letters lie within the phrase

parts.note: the run straddles the two words

explanation.surface: The swine flu comes back and shows the mood of people in Goa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' suggests morale, but it is a distilled drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Feni is a spirit distilled in Goa from cashew apples or coconut sap.

clue.text: More work on society getting to top of the tree? Could be me

definitions.note: the clue as a whole describes the visionary

parts.note: Utopia is Sir Thomas More's famous book
S for society

indicators.note: the top of a word in an across clue is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of tree

explanation.surface: Someone works harder on social climbing to reach the pinnacle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More work' looks like extra effort, but it is the book by Thomas More.
explanation.definitionFit: A utopiast is an idealist who dreams of perfect societies, and the setter jokes that he may be one.

clue.text: Your setter's eaten out in small cafe

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Mephisto setter Tim Moorey, so Tim's
taken as written

explanation.surface: The setter has gone out for a meal at a little café.
explanation.walkthrough: Mephisto setters sign off by name; this week's was Tim Moorey.
explanation.definitionFit: An estaminet is a small French café or bar, familiar to British soldiers in the First World War.
